purpose: Checks for a left/right preference lean
takeaway: Overall 54% of decisive responses chose the right-hand method, but in the 20 pairs without an original 65% chose the left, so the lean follows which version is shown (refactors were usually on the right) rather than the side of the screen.

purpose: Shows the heavily skewed distributions and the concentration of methods at small values
takeaway: In the 4.4 million main-corpus methods most measurements are tiny (64% have CC 1, 63% have CogC 0, 67% have MaxNest 0) with very long tails; the plot is descriptive and no distribution is fitted.

purpose: Broader metric correlation matrix
takeaway: Broader set of corpus metrics: control-flow metrics (CC, CogC, nesting) form one very tight group and size metrics (LOC, words, Halstead) another; the two groups are related to each other at about 0.7, while naming and comment measures are only weakly related to either.

purpose: PCA biplot: corpus density (30,000-method sample), loadings of the four metrics, and the 34 survey snippets (originals orange, variants blue); dashed ellipse holds 90% of corpus methods; only snippets outside it are labelled
takeaway: On the first two principal components (96% of the variance), 11 of the 34 survey snippets lie outside the ellipse holding 90% of corpus methods, and all four metric arrows point the same way along PC1.

purpose: Scree for the broader metric sets
takeaway: With the broader metric sets the first component explains about half of the variation in the corpus sample (52%), so the broader set carries more than one dimension.

purpose: PCA loadings
takeaway: What each principal component of the four key metrics is made of; the sign of a whole component is arbitrary.

purpose: PCA score plots
takeaway: Corpus methods and survey snippets plotted on the first two components (the survey snippets span the range of the typical corpus method but are not a random sample).

purpose: Broader metric correlation matrix for the survey snippets
takeaway: Correlations among the broader set of measurements for the 34 survey snippets.

purpose: Response-level tie share (differs from the pair-level share)
takeaway: Response-level version of the tie share: because pairs differ in how many people saw them, it differs from the pair-level share.

purpose: The metric correlations once the trivial lowest-value methods are removed
takeaway: Without the methods at each metric's lowest value the corpus correlations fall but stay positive: CC and CogC 0.92, MaxNest 0.64 to 0.76 with the other control-flow metrics, LOC 0.73 to 0.74 with CC and CogC and 0.53 with MaxNest; in the 29 to 32 survey snippets that remain they range from 0.36 (CC with MaxNest) to 0.90 (CogC with MaxNest).

purpose: Same test on 1,000,000 random pairs of corpus methods
takeaway: For random pairs of corpus methods the metrics order a pair in opposite directions in under 6% of pairs; the main difference is ties, since most random pairs are trivial and CC, CogC and MaxNest often tie.

purpose: Resolution in the corpus
takeaway: Two random corpus methods tie on CC 44% of the time, on CogC 43%, on MaxNest 50% and on LOC only 12%, because most methods are tiny.

purpose: Resolution in the corpus once the trivial lowest-value methods are removed
takeaway: Once methods at a metric's lowest value (CC 1, CogC 0, LOC 1, MaxNest 0) are removed, two random corpus methods tie on CC 20% of the time, CogC 18%, LOC 13% and MaxNest 48%, so most of the CC and CogC ties in fig04b come from trivial methods but MaxNest still ties often.

purpose: Supporting evidence: how much variation one shared component captures (not proof the metrics are equivalent)
takeaway: One shared component explains 89% of the variation between the four metrics in the corpus and 80% in the 34 constructed survey snippets; this is supporting evidence and does not show the metrics are equivalent.

purpose: How strongly the metrics' rankings agree, in the corpus and in the survey snippets
takeaway: CC and CogC rank corpus methods almost identically (Spearman 0.99) and MaxNest is close to both (0.94), while LOC is related at about 0.72; the 34 constructed survey snippets show weaker relationships, especially between CC and MaxNest.

purpose: Direct test of the supervisor's definition on the survey pairs
takeaway: In the 44 survey pairs the metrics almost never order a pair in opposite directions (0-7% of pairs, never for CC and CogC); most differences are one metric tying while the other separates.

purpose: Same test restricted to non-trivial methods (CC >= 3)
takeaway: Among non-trivial methods (CC >= 3) CC and CogC mostly agree on direction (70% concordant, 8% discordant), while LOC is discordant with CC, CogC and MaxNest in 15% to 18% of pairs and MaxNest ties on many pairs the others separate.

purpose: Resolution: how often each metric cannot tell the two survey methods apart
takeaway: CC ties on 41% of the survey pairs and MaxNest on 36%, against 18% for CogC and LOC.

purpose: The seven pairs where CC, CogC, LOC and MaxNest all tie: share of decisive responses preferring the later version, with Wilson 95% CIs per pair and the pooled participant-bootstrap estimate in red; dashed line = 50%
takeaway: On the seven pairs where all four metrics tie, 81% of decisive responses (61 of 75) chose the later version as less complex; six of the seven pairs are above 50% and one (Q5C, naming) is at 50%.

purpose: Latent perceived complexity of each snippet from the within-task ordinal Bradley-Terry model (95% Wald intervals)
takeaway: In the within-task Bradley-Terry model most variants are judged less complex than their original, 03-V2 is judged more complex (+0.9, interval above zero) and 05-V3 is indistinguishable from its original (+0.1); within tasks the latent scores track MaxNest (rho 0.87), CogC (0.82), LOC (0.73) and CC (0.60) in that order.

purpose: Commit rate against direction accuracy for CC, CogC, LOC and MaxNest (95% participant-bootstrap intervals; dashed line = 50%)
takeaway: CC and MaxNest separate 63% and 66% of the pairs participants took a side on, against 86% for CogC and LOC, while direction accuracy is similar for all four (CC 69%, CogC 72%, LOC 68%, MaxNest 75%, intervals overlapping): the agreement gap comes from separating the pair, not from direction.

purpose: Full five-way decomposition of agreement
takeaway: All 750 responses split five ways by what the metric and the participant each said; the main figures show the two parts that matter (fig07a, fig07b).

purpose: Chance-corrected agreement (kappa)
takeaway: Cohen's kappa for each metric (0 = no better than chance): CogC 0.27, LOC 0.21, MaxNest 0.21, CC 0.14, all with intervals above zero; the same idea as the chance diamond in fig06.

purpose: Leave-one-task-out agreement for the four metrics; each dot is labelled with the task that was dropped, the diamond is the full-data value
takeaway: Dropping any one of the 10 tasks keeps CogC the highest-agreeing metric (54% to 59% across the drops) and keeps the order CogC > LOC > MaxNest > CC in 9 of 10; the CogC-minus-LOC gap falls to 0.3 points when task 3 is dropped.

purpose: Agreement against tie rate for the 13 measures in fig06b; the four key metrics are coloured
takeaway: Across the 13 measures, agreement falls as the tie rate rises (Halstead effort and CogC tie on about 11% and 15% and agree on 58% and 57%; CC ties on 36% and agrees on 43%; parameter count ties on 100% and agrees on 10%).

purpose: Coefficients of CC, CogC, LOC and MaxNest in the cumulative-link mixed model of the 1-5 ratings (all four entered together)
takeaway: With all four metrics in one cumulative-link mixed model only MaxNest's coefficient excludes zero (3.1, 95% CI 1.4 to 4.9); CogC is borderline (2.1, -0.1 to 4.2) and CC and LOC are indistinguishable from zero, but the predictors are correlated up to 0.84 so each coefficient is imprecise.

purpose: Optional: agreement with participants for every measurement recorded for the survey snippets, including Halstead
takeaway: Across every measurement recorded for the survey snippets, Halstead effort (58%) and CogC (57%) agree with participants most often, with overlapping intervals; CC (43%) is the lowest of the size and structure measurements, and fan-out, identifier words, comments, Javadoc, recursion and parameter count are close to the agreement expected by chance.

purpose: 3x3 grid for CC vs LOC: where the two metrics agree or differ, and which side participants took
takeaway: Where CC ties and LOC separates (11 pairs) participants took LOC's side in 66% of decisive responses; in the two pairs where they point in opposite directions the split (57% CC, 43% LOC) is not significant.

purpose: 3x3 grid for CC vs MaxNest: where the two metrics agree or differ, and which side participants took
takeaway: No pair has CC and MaxNest pointing in opposite directions; where CC ties and MaxNest separates (7 pairs) participants took MaxNest's side in 82% of decisive responses, but where MaxNest ties and CC separates (5 pairs) only 52% took CC's side.

purpose: 3x3 grid for CogC vs LOC: where the two metrics agree or differ, and which side participants took
takeaway: CogC and LOC point in opposite directions on three pairs, where participants sided with CogC in 66% of decisive responses (not significant after correction for multiple tests).

purpose: 3x3 grid for CogC vs MaxNest: where the two metrics agree or differ, and which side participants took
takeaway: CogC and MaxNest point in opposite directions on a single pair, where participants sided with CogC in 88% of decisive responses; this rests on one pair.

purpose: 3x3 grid for LOC vs MaxNest: where the two metrics agree or differ, and which side participants took
takeaway: No pair has LOC and MaxNest pointing in opposite directions; where MaxNest ties and LOC separates (8 pairs) participants took LOC's side in 46% of decisive responses.

purpose: Pair-level view (each pair counted once) of whether measurement differences track perceived differences
takeaway: Counting each pair once, every metric's measurement difference correlates positively with the perceived difference (Spearman 0.51 for CC to 0.70 for MaxNest).

purpose: Shows the ranking of metrics under alternative inclusion rules
takeaway: Dropping participants who missed screening questions changes agreement by under one point; dropping tied or No-difference responses raises every metric's agreement and changes the ranking (MaxNest is highest among pairs it separates), so overall agreement and direction accuracy tell different stories.

purpose: Checks whether agreement differs by self-reported experience
takeaway: Agreement rises with self-reported experience for all four metrics, but not significantly after correction (Holm p = .38), and the 'none' (5) and 'large' (3) groups are very small.

purpose: Headline RQ2 result: which metrics agree most with participants, and how far above chance
takeaway: CogC agrees with participants most often (57% of 750 responses) and CC least (43%); every metric is above the agreement expected by chance (black diamond), CC by the smallest margin.

purpose: Shows how much of each metric's disagreement is tying versus pointing the other way
takeaway: When a participant chose a side, CC tied on 37% of those responses and MaxNest on 34%, against 15% for CogC and 14% for LOC; the share of responses where a metric pointed the other way was similar for all four (16-27%).

purpose: Direction accuracy of each metric when it does separate the pair
takeaway: When a metric does separate the two methods and the participant chooses a side, all four metrics are right about 70% of the time (68-75%), so CC's lower overall agreement comes from tying, not from pointing the wrong way.

purpose: Pairs where CC ties and CogC, MaxNest or LOC separates: share of decisive responses choosing the method that metric rates lower (Wilson 95% CIs per pair; pooled participant-bootstrap estimate in red)
takeaway: Where CC ties but CogC separates the pair (10 pairs), 83% of decisive responses (123 of 149) chose the method CogC rates lower, and 9 of the 10 pairs are above 50%; the same holds for MaxNest (83%, 6 of 7 pairs) and LOC (66%, 8 of 11 pairs).

purpose: Agreement split by whether the metric ties and where the lower measurement was shown
takeaway: Every metric agrees much more often when the lower measurement is on the left (A) than on the right (B), and only about 10% of the time when it ties, because a tie can agree only with 'No difference'.

purpose: How often each metric ties on the pair, by the participant's answer (no difference / slightly / much); exported 1568 px wide
takeaway: CC ties about as often when participants saw a big difference (37%) as when they saw none (35%), whereas CogC, LOC and MaxNest tie less often on the pairs participants rated 'much' different (11%, 9% and 27%) than on those rated 'slightly' different (17%, 18% and 39%).

purpose: Scatter behind the reduction-vs-preference result
takeaway: Pair by pair, larger reductions in a measurement do not reliably go with larger perceived improvements (Spearman -0.17 to 0.36, none significant after correction).

purpose: Win-rate leaderboard shaded by each version's CC within its task, to see whether higher measurements go with being judged more complex
takeaway: Versions with the highest CC in their task were judged less complex in 40% of comparisons on average, against 66% for those with the lowest CC (Spearman -0.54 across the 34 versions, descriptive).

purpose: Win-rate leaderboard shaded by each version's CogC within its task, to see whether higher measurements go with being judged more complex
takeaway: Versions with the highest CogC in their task were judged less complex in 34% of comparisons on average, against 70% for those with the lowest CogC (Spearman -0.74 across the 34 versions, descriptive).

purpose: Win-rate leaderboard shaded by each version's LOC within its task, to see whether higher measurements go with being judged more complex
takeaway: Versions with the highest LOC in their task were judged less complex in 37% of comparisons on average, against 67% for those with the lowest LOC (Spearman -0.60 across the 34 versions, descriptive).

purpose: Win-rate leaderboard shaded by each version's MaxNest within its task, to see whether higher measurements go with being judged more complex
takeaway: Versions with the highest MaxNest in their task were judged less complex in 34% of comparisons on average, against 68% for those with the lowest MaxNest (Spearman -0.75 across the 34 versions, descriptive).

purpose: Descriptive view of which kinds of change were preferred
takeaway: Removing branching or nesting, and adding comments, were the changes preferred most; extraction and naming changed perceptions little, and shortening code while keeping CC and CogC (volume) or replacing recursion with a loop made code feel more complex. Descriptive: each kind of change rests on one to four variants.

purpose: Ranks every version by how often participants judged it less complex
takeaway: 14 of 24 refactored variants were judged less complex more often than not, against 1 of 10 originals (03-ORIG); clear exceptions are 03-ORIG, which won, and 03-V2, a refactor that lost.

purpose: Direct test, pair by pair, of whether each refactor was preferred to its original
takeaway: After correction for multiple tests four refactors were significantly preferred to their original and one (03-V2) was significantly rejected; the rest are inconclusive, mostly because many pairs have few responses.

purpose: Whether refactors that lowered a measurement were preferred more than those that did not
takeaway: Refactors were preferred in roughly two thirds of decisive responses whether or not a metric's measurement fell (for example CC 65% when it fell and 71% when unchanged), so a falling measurement did not clearly mean a stronger preference.
